To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a cold-insoluble protein fraction of human and bovine plasma contains fibrinogen as a major component, that the fibrinogen is present as aggregates and oligomers, that the oligomers are resistant to urea and that the aggregates are dissociated by 6 M ure.

the cold-insolubility of fibrinogen is due to intermolecular cross- linking of its peptide chains and that the cold-insolu- ble fraction is a mixture of fibril aggregates, fibrinogen, and a small amount of an unidentified protein.
the cold-insolubility of fibrinogen is caused by the formation of aggregates which are dissociated at high pH or in the presence of urea.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the isolation of the cold-insuble fibrinogen and the detection of oligomeric and monomeric protein components of this fraction.
the isolation, characterization and formation of cold-insoluble aggregates of fibrinogen.

the identification and characterization of a cold-insoluble, oligomeric fibrinogen fraction and with the demonstration that the formation of fibrin aggregates in the presence of fibrin monomers can lead to the formation of oligomeric fibrillogenesis products.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
fibrinogen in plasma exists in a state of aggregation which is sensitive to ionic strength and pH and which can be dissociated in 2 M glycine and 6 M ureas.
fibrinogen is not a single protein but a complex of proteins with different molecular weights, different solubility properties, and different susceptibilities to proteolytic degradation.

cold-insoluble aggregates of fibrinogen, as well as of fibrin, are formed in vitro and that the fibrinogen fraction insoluble in 2.1 m glycine at 4°C is a mixture of fibrillar fibrinogen, fibrin monomers and aggregates of fibrin and fibrinogen.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
fibrinogen aggregates and oligomers can be formed in vitro and in vivo and are present in the cold-insolubles.
the cold-insolubility of fibrinogen is caused by the formation of a variety of aggregates, some of which may represent covalently cross-linked oligomers.
the cold-insolubility of bovine and to a minor extent of human fibrinogen is due to the presence of a large amount of aggregated material which dissociated upon addition of 6 M Urea.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cold-insolubility of fibrinogen is not caused by intermolecular crosslinks but by the aggregation of fibrinogen molecules.
cold-insoluble fractions of bovine and of human plasma contain fibrinogen aggregates.
fibrinogen is a very complex protein and that its cold-insoluble precipitate may contain a variety of different aggregates and oligomeric forms.
